rv.q: Brasch’s honest, heartfelt (and semi-autobiographical) writing -- coupled with the sublime work of some of New York’s finest actors -- make this a must-see play, rather than a must-avoid one.
A terrific Noah Galvin, buttressed by a perfect ensemble of top-notch castmates

“The Reservoir” may not glitter as brightly overall; Mr. Brasch could have cut a good half hour, starting with some of Jake’s often too-cute, navel-gazing asides. But its heart, and the marvelous cast here, make it worth diving in.
Jake Brasch’s The Reservoir at times seems long as it has so many short vignettes but ultimately wraps up the story in a neat package.
Were it not for Galvin’s simplicity and charm, this situation could feel way too emotionally exploitative, and stressful.
Then again, he doesn’t make us feel that Josh is ever in any real danger.
But that feeling of disappointing those that we love did cling with me for days after experiencing this beautifully aching piece.
The Reservoir finds surprising humor amid the harsh realities of alcoholism and Alzheimer’s.
Unfortunately, those veteran performers are not playing characters so much as archetypes in a play that purports to deal with serious issues but never gets beneath the surface.
It is a chaotic place, occasionally exhausting, often hilarious, and unexpectedly full of love.
“The Reservoir” is a theatrically inventive, intellectually rigorous, emotionally earned meditation on memory, recovery, and mortality.
Galvin delivers a star-making performance that recalls the work of the young Matthew Broderick.
The audience may feel the same way.
But if you find the cute but irrelevant and obvious jokes tiring, you may discover that after two hours and fifteen minutes, you’ve had more than enough.

cn.t: Critics find this addiction-and-Alzheimer's dramedy surprisingly funny, with Noah Galvin delivering a standout performance that elevates Jake Brasch's autobiographical play, though some feel the sitcom-style approach undermines weightier themes.
